news.title: iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Review: I Keep Coming Back to the Pro
news.summary: The last couple years have been big for iPhone. In 2025, Apple introduced two brand new iPhone models: iPhone 16e, an entry-level model with most of the essential components of the more expensive iPhones of its generation; and iPhone Air, the thinnest-ever iPhone to date at the time. This year, Apple announced the iPhone Duo, the company's first-ever foldable iPhone and with it, a whole new form factor and way of using iPhone as we know it. In between the new iPhone models, Apple has, year-by-year, continued the steady evolution of its Pro and Pro Max phones. This year, for the first time, I had the opportunity to review both iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. One of the devices was a review unit on loan from Apple, whilst the other was the phone I purchased for myself. Being able to use both devices, one after the other, gave me a unique opportunity to evaluate them side-by-side, and I have a much deeper appreciation for each model and its strengths (and limitations). And after spending time with each phone, I came away with a surprising and yet inevitable conclusion: while iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are similar, they are very different devices for very different use cases. And only one of them is a device I would routinely recommend for most people. Getting a Feel for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max On the surface, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are almost identical to last year's devices. Cosmic Orange is out in favor of Burgundy and Glacier [light blue], but on the outside at least, not much else has changed. iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max come in Black, Silver, Glacier [light blue], and Burgundy. Both devices have a Super Retina XDR display with Ceramic Shield 2; forged unibody featuring an Apple-designed 7000 series aluminum alloy; and a color-matched glass back with Ceramic Shield. iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display, while the display on iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. (Displays are measured diagonally.) The left edge of the device houses the Volume Buttons. The right edge of the device has the Side Button at the top and the Camera Control towards the bottom. The bottom edge of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max holds the bottom speaker on the left, a USB-C port in the middle, and the microphone on the right. There are three different cameras on the top back of the device, housed in the plateau. The plateau extends across approximately the top third of the back of the device. The back glass feels very similar in texture to the forged unibody. In my hand—that all-important ‘hand-feel’—iPhone 18 Pro feels, as Goldilocks would say, ‘just right’. It is appropriately heavy—‘substantial’—and is neither so big such that holding it one-handed is likely to be difficult for most; nor is it so small that one must compromise on battery life or overall form and function. Whereas iPhone 18 Pro feels ideal for most, iPhone 18 Pro Max is absolutely huge in comparison and almost feels unwieldy. It is heavy in the hand and even heavier in the pocket of my khakis. One-handed usage is not really an option, though if you are already used to and comfortable with the Pro Max phones, do note that iPhone 18 Pro Max has not changed in size. Battery Life iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback with up to 24 hours of typical usage per charge, while iPhone 18 Pro Max offers up to 45 hours of video playback and up to 30 hours of typical usage per charge. In my experience, battery life on even the smaller iPhone 18 Pro has been enough to get me through the day, and then some. On a typical day, I finished with around 40% battery remaining on iPhone 18 Pro and 60% on iPhone 18 Pro Max, give or take. The lowest I got the iPhone 18 Pro was 21% on my very first full day with the device, and the lowest I got the 18 Pro Max was 32% on a day when, unbeknownst to me, screen brightness got set to 100% and Screen Curtain became disabled. Not counting the days when the erroneous settings were a factor, my next-lowest end-of-day battery reading on iPhone 18 Pro Max was 46% after a little over 18 hours off the charger. On one day with exceptionally light usage, I finished at 64% with iPhone 18 Pro and 81% with iPhone 18 Pro Max. Performance iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max both share Apple’s latest and greatest A20 Pro processor and an improved cooling system. While I do not use my phones for processor-intensive work, what I can say is that day-to-day performance of the A20 Pro is as good as you could possibly want it to be. Apps and screens open quickly, and the operating system runs well. VoiceOver—Apple’s built-in screen reader for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision users—responds as soon as I touch the screen. There is no latency whatsoever. When compared to last year’s A19 Pro, in day-to-day device usage, I noticed hardly any difference with this year's A20 Pro in iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. The A19 series of processors already ran iOS 27 and VoiceOver exceptionally well, with Apple definitely appearing to have done some serious work to make VoiceOver feel more snappy. Usually, when one installs a new major update, there is a small decrease in VoiceOver responsiveness; this was not the case for me this year running iOS 27 on iPhone 17 Pro Max. (I also tested several of the iOS 27 betas on an iPhone 17e with the regular A19 processor, and my experience was the same.) Given that performance of the A19 Pro was already incredibly good in everyday usage, it should come as no surprise then that this year’s A20 Pro is only nominally better for the same types of work. It is hard to improve on excellent, but companies of course will (and should) try. In terms of device heat, I cannot honestly say that I noticed any huge reduction in heat under load between iPhone 17 Pro Max and this year's models, except on my first couple days with iPhone 18 Pro. Comparing between iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro did anecdotally seem to be more prone to getting warmer quicker, though that extra warmth may have been caused by a particular third-party app. Speakers and Sound When I shared my initial impressions of iPhone 18 Pro ahead of the launch, I wrote about how much I liked the sound from the device’s speaker. My week with the device confirmed my initial experience: whether listening to VoiceOver or music, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro sound full, warm, balanced, and are all around a joy to listen to. iPhone 18 Pro Max is a bit more of a mixed bag. Compared to iPhone 18 Pro, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max have much more bass, more high end, and... Less of the midrange warmth that makes the iPhone 18 Pro sound so good overall. Going from iPhone 18 Pro to iPhone 18 Pro Max, I was, honestly, disappointed. It's not all bad, though. While my primary point of reference for speaker quality is VoiceOver speech and other spoken audio, the very things that make iPhone 18 Pro Max sound so poor with spoken audio are what make it stand out with music. When listening to music, iPhone 18 Pro Max outshines the smaller iPhone 18 Pro: there is more bass, more high end, and certainly more volume. While I wouldn't say that the sound is room-filling by any stretch of the imagination, it is quite loud at close range and more than enough to replace a small Bluetooth speaker. Siri AI While not specifically a new feature of this year's iPhones, Siri got a major upgrade in iOS 27. Since updating, I find myself using Siri a lot more for things I would have previously needed to use a third-party description app or AI service for. Asking research-based questions is an obvious one, but it goes beyond that. For example, whilst waiting for the arrival of my Apple Watch Series 12, I asked Siri to tell me where the delivery was on the map. I have also used Siri AI to describe weather graphics posted on Facebook, which is especially helpful as Siri AI can access my contextual information that Apple's Intelligent Image Descriptions or third-party tools cannot. "Where is that line of thunderstorms relative to me?" is a question that Siri AI can answer with access to my location, and I find the descriptions of what's onscreen to be sufficiently detailed and helpful. And yet, Siri AI is not as good as it could be. My experiences using AI services like ChatGPT to vibecode and do other tasks using natural language sometimes left me disappointed with Siri AI. Since Siri AI is integrated right into the operating system, it should be able to do everything that I can accomplish through navigating the UI manually. And so far at least, this has not been the case. Camera, Cellular, and Other Things One of the headline new features of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is the 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture. Being blind, I am not able to speak firsthand to this and, while I had a very interesting discussion with ChatGPT on variable aperture and what this might mean in practical terms, I am not comfortable including any of that here as I cannot independently verify its accuracy. For an in-depth evaluation of the iPhone 18 Pro camera specifically, I recommend this review by PetaPixel's Jaron Schneider. iPhone 18 Pro (specifically) has the Apple C2 modem, and both models have the Apple N1 wireless networking chip. In my speed tests, the only meaningful difference between the C2 modem in iPhone 18 Pro and the modem in iPhone 18 Pro Max was that the C2 on iPhone 18 Pro seemed to deliver upload speeds that were slightly faster. Testing was done on the T-Mobile network in Chicago. As spotted by AppleVis user Zach M, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max support 8-dot braille in Braille Screen Input (BSI), and calibration of braille dots in BSI now works similar to how it is on iPad. Not being familiar with 8-dot braille, I cannot speak to this firsthand. Due to the size of its battery, iPhone 18 Pro Max has a "Prepare to Ship" option that one must use to sufficiently discharge the battery and limit battery capacity prior to shipping it for repair or any other reason. This Apple Support Article has more info. With a compatible adapter, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max can charge up to 50% in 15 minutes. While I do not think I have the prerequisite adapter for this, my own subjective experience is that charging is faster than on last year's model. Which Phone Should I Buy? As I see it, my role as a reviewer is to evaluate a phone and make purchasing recommendations in terms of how I think most people are likely to use it; rather than assessing based on my own preferences which are very specific and unique to me. As such, you may have noticed that up to this point, I have tried to keep my opinions focused on what I feel are the strengths and weaknesses of each device (rather than what "I" like in a phone). This was intentional. My goal in my reviews is to give you information and let you come to your own conclusions. Complicating any attempt at a meaningful recommendation that will withstand the test of time is that we are just beginning the 2026-27 iPhone release cycle, with more releases likely on the way throughout the next six or so months. iPhone Duo is going to be available for preorder next week, with customer availability beginning October 23. The more I learn about and consider iPhone Duo, the more I am realizing that it is going to be unlike anything we have seen before. iPhone Duo is something completely new, with a new form factor and user experience. Watch this space. With all of that in mind, I think that iPhone 18 Pro is likely to be the best iPhone for most people in the 2026-27 cycle. The size of iPhone 18 Pro is 'just right', and the battery will likely get you through the day (if not more). Performance is equally good no matter which model you choose. And while the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max definitely have more bass and high end, iPhone 18 Pro sounds better and more natural overall, and it is the device I would myself prefer to listen to long-term. Of course, there are some people for whom iPhone 18 Pro Max is an easy recommendation. If like me you want the absolute best battery life possible, iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only phone to get. Likewise, iPhone 18 Pro Max is also a strong contender for people with low vision, though the iPhone Duo I think will be the winner in that category with its 7.6-inch inner display. I just would not recommend iPhone 18 Pro Max for someone whose top priority is sound quality of VoiceOver or other spoken audio, or if you value being able to hold and use your device easily in one hand. If you want a new iPhone but the 18 Pro/Max and Duo are not in your budget, consider that Apple has over the last couple years released budget-oriented iPhone models in the early part of the year. If the past couple years are any indicator, these devices will likely include a current-generation A20-series processor, so day-to-day performance will likely be on par with the Pro/Max and Duo for everyday use. When buying a new iPhone, there are a couple of things I would actively caution you against. First, I would not recommend buying an older iPhone model (including the currently available iPhone Air, iPhone 17, and iPhone 17e), as these devices have older processors. While software support on older devices is very good (iOS 27, for example, will run on the 2019 iPhone 11 series), Apple has historically ended software support one processor generation at a time. Put another way: an iPhone 18 is likely to get one more year of software updates than is the iPhone 17 series and original iPhone Air, as these devices have last year's A19-series processors. The other thing I encourage caution with is carrier iPhone promos. While these programs can provide great-looking offers up front, I am of the opinion that carrier promos are primarily meant to benefit the carrier and keep the customer locked in and paying. If buying from your carrier, make sure the math works out and it really is in your best interest. Depending on your location, Apple may offer financing and upgrade options, so you could buy on installments directly from Apple and avoid your carrier entirely. Lastly, if you want a refurbished iPhone, stick to devices certified refurbished by Apple. If you buy a refurbished device from Apple, you are guaranteed a certain level of quality that you may not easily find on the used market. Conclusion On the day I published this review, I did something surprising: I transferred all of my data and my cellular plans back onto iPhone 18 Pro. As much as I love the battery life of iPhone 18 Pro Max, I kept being drawn back to iPhone 18 Pro for its size, form factor, 'holdability', and great-sounding speakers. While my personal preference is and will always be for the phone with the largest battery, iPhone 18 Pro really is, I think, the best iPhone for most people this year. I really do like it.

It is hard to improve on excellent, but companies of course will (and should) try.

In terms of device heat, I cannot honestly say that I noticed any huge reduction in heat under load between iPhone 17 Pro Max and this year's models, except on my first couple days with iPhone 18 Pro. Comparing between iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro did anecdotally seem to be more prone to getting warmer quicker, though that extra warmth may have been caused by a particular third-party app.

When I shared my initial impressions of iPhone 18 Pro ahead of the launch, I wrote about how much I liked the sound from the device’s speaker. My week with the device confirmed my initial experience: whether listening to VoiceOver or music, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro sound full, warm, balanced, and are all around a joy to listen to.

iPhone 18 Pro Max is a bit more of a mixed bag. Compared to iPhone 18 Pro, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max have much more bass, more high end, and... Less of the midrange warmth that makes the iPhone 18 Pro sound so good overall. Going from iPhone 18 Pro to iPhone 18 Pro Max, I was, honestly, disappointed.

It's not all bad, though. While my primary point of reference for speaker quality is VoiceOver speech and other spoken audio, the very things that make iPhone 18 Pro Max sound so poor with spoken audio are what make it stand out with music. When listening to music, iPhone 18 Pro Max outshines the smaller iPhone 18 Pro: there is more bass, more high end, and certainly more volume. While I wouldn't say that the sound is room-filling by any stretch of the imagination, it is quite loud at close range and more than enough to replace a small Bluetooth speaker.

While not specifically a new feature of this year's iPhones, Siri got a major upgrade in iOS 27. Since updating, I find myself using Siri a lot more for things I would have previously needed to use a third-party description app or AI service for. Asking research-based questions is an obvious one, but it goes beyond that. For example, whilst waiting for the arrival of my Apple Watch Series 12, I asked Siri to tell me where the delivery was on the map. I have also used Siri AI to describe weather graphics posted on Facebook, which is especially helpful as Siri AI can access my contextual information that Apple's Intelligent Image Descriptions or third-party tools cannot. "Where is that line of thunderstorms relative to me?" is a question that Siri AI can answer with access to my location, and I find the descriptions of what's onscreen to be sufficiently detailed and helpful.

And yet, Siri AI is not as good as it could be. My experiences using AI services like ChatGPT to vibecode and do other tasks using natural language sometimes left me disappointed with Siri AI. Since Siri AI is integrated right into the operating system, it should be able to do everything that I can accomplish through navigating the UI manually. And so far at least, this has not been the case.

As I see it, my role as a reviewer is to evaluate a phone and make purchasing recommendations in terms of how I think most people are likely to use it; rather than assessing based on my own preferences which are very specific and unique to me. As such, you may have noticed that up to this point, I have tried to keep my opinions focused on what I feel are the strengths and weaknesses of each device (rather than what "I" like in a phone). This was intentional. My goal in my reviews is to give you information and let you come to your own conclusions.

Complicating any attempt at a meaningful recommendation that will withstand the test of time is that we are just beginning the 2026-27 iPhone release cycle, with more releases likely on the way throughout the next six or so months. iPhone Duo is going to be available for preorder next week, with customer availability beginning October 23. The more I learn about and consider iPhone Duo, the more I am realizing that it is going to be unlike anything we have seen before. iPhone Duo is something completely new, with a new form factor and user experience. Watch this space.

With all of that in mind, I think that iPhone 18 Pro is likely to be the best iPhone for most people in the 2026-27 cycle. The size of iPhone 18 Pro is 'just right', and the battery will likely get you through the day (if not more). Performance is equally good no matter which model you choose. And while the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max definitely have more bass and high end, iPhone 18 Pro sounds better and more natural overall, and it is the device I would myself prefer to listen to long-term.

Of course, there are some people for whom iPhone 18 Pro Max is an easy recommendation. If like me you want the absolute best battery life possible, iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only phone to get. Likewise, iPhone 18 Pro Max is also a strong contender for people with low vision, though the iPhone Duo I think will be the winner in that category with its 7.6-inch inner display. I just would not recommend iPhone 18 Pro Max for someone whose top priority is sound quality of VoiceOver or other spoken audio, or if you value being able to hold and use your device easily in one hand.

If you want a new iPhone but the 18 Pro/Max and Duo are not in your budget, consider that Apple has over the last couple years released budget-oriented iPhone models in the early part of the year. If the past couple years are any indicator, these devices will likely include a current-generation A20-series processor, so day-to-day performance will likely be on par with the Pro/Max and Duo for everyday use.

When buying a new iPhone, there are a couple of things I would actively caution you against. First, I would not recommend buying an older iPhone model (including the currently available iPhone Air, iPhone 17, and iPhone 17e), as these devices have older processors. While software support on older devices is very good (iOS 27, for example, will run on the 2019 iPhone 11 series), Apple has historically ended software support one processor generation at a time. Put another way: an iPhone 18 is likely to get one more year of software updates than is the iPhone 17 series and original iPhone Air, as these devices have last year's A19-series processors.

The other thing I encourage caution with is carrier iPhone promos. While these programs can provide great-looking offers up front, I am of the opinion that carrier promos are primarily meant to benefit the carrier and keep the customer locked in and paying. If buying from your carrier, make sure the math works out and it really is in your best interest. Depending on your location, Apple may offer financing and upgrade options, so you could buy on installments directly from Apple and avoid your carrier entirely.

Lastly, if you want a refurbished iPhone, stick to devices certified refurbished by Apple. If you buy a refurbished device from Apple, you are guaranteed a certain level of quality that you may not easily find on the used market.

On the day I published this review, I did something surprising: I transferred all of my data and my cellular plans back onto iPhone 18 Pro. As much as I love the battery life of iPhone 18 Pro Max, I kept being drawn back to iPhone 18 Pro for its size, form factor, 'holdability', and great-sounding speakers. While my personal preference is and will always be for the phone with the largest battery, iPhone 18 Pro really is, I think, the best iPhone for most people this year. I really do like it.

news.title: Third-Party Screen Readers: Are They a Security Risk?
news.summary: Unlike iOS, Android allows third-party apps to request accessibility permission, which makes it possible to develop screen readers for Android rather than limiting blind users…
news.body:
Published 7 October 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Unlike iOS, Android allows third-party apps to request accessibility permission, which makes it possible to develop screen readers for Android rather than limiting blind users to the built-in screen reader, TalkBack.

The presence of third-party screen readers has helped compensate for the lack of features and responsiveness issues in TalkBack. However, for a screen reader to work, it needs to be granted accessibility permission, which comes with powerful privileges that can pose serious risks if they fall into the wrong hands. The risks that come with granting accessibility permission, as well as the gains it provides, and the balance between security and openness, have been hot topics throughout the years. With the growing popularity of third-party screen readers, including new ones being developed recently with the help of AI-assisted vibe coding, the security aspect is becoming increasingly important to discuss and understand so that users can make informed decisions.

Before going any further, I want to state from the outset that the goal of this article is neither to give clearance to any screen reader or service, nor to accuse another of wrongdoing.

Table of Contents

The following definition is taken directly from the Android Developers website :

“An accessibility service is an app that enhances the user interface to assist users with disabilities or who might temporarily be unable to fully interact with a device. These services run in the background and communicate with the system to inspect screen content and interact with apps on the user’s behalf. Examples include screen readers (like TalkBack), Switch Access tools, and voice control systems.”

An article titled Accessibility Service – An Android Blessing and a Security Challenge in the Same Package from Bitdefender states:

“Android’s accessibility service is a powerful tool that allows people with disabilities to use mobile devices more easily. It’s also a favorite among criminals seeking to take over a device because it holds so much power.”

When granting an app permission to act as an accessibility service, the user gives the app access to powerful capabilities, including:

Although accessibility permission is built for services like screen readers, which are the focus of this article, it is also used by other apps to enable features that would not otherwise be possible. It is a core element of the popular automation app Tasker, and some launchers include an optional accessibility service to gain additional privileges.

Criminals and other bad actors have also found a great opportunity in accessibility services, which they try to seize and exploit to the fullest.

Google did not stay on the sidelines for long, taking active steps to make exploiting accessibility permission harder.

Since 2021, apps that use the AccessibilityService API have been required to provide additional information about their use of the API through Google Play’s accessibility declaration process before approval. Starting with Android 13, apps that are not installed from Google Play cannot simply be granted access to restricted settings, including accessibility access, by enabling the service from Accessibility settings. Instead, the user must first allow restricted settings for the app from its App info page and confirm the choice. Apps installed through some third-party installers can still bypass this step at the time of writing.

Google even restricts the use of unverified accessibility services when Advanced Protection is enabled, a mode intended for users who may face a higher security risk or who place a particularly high priority on privacy and security.

As stated above, granting any app the accessibility permission comes with a lot of privileges. However, in order for a screen reader to work, it must be granted accessibility permission. Without granting it this access, the screen reader is essentially useless, as its core functionality relies on the accessibility service it has.

Despite improvements, TalkBack on Android lacks many features that other screen readers provide. Many users find that third-party screen readers are more responsive compared to TalkBack, which still lags when performing certain tasks, such as scrolling, or on specific devices, especially those with mid-range or low-end processors. In fact, better responsiveness is an advantage that most developers of other screen readers use to advertise their apps.

No matter how we phrase it, granting any app accessibility service privileges poses a potential risk, even if the app is blocked from accessing the internet. However, this doesn’t mean that the app is really a risk, or that it is built with the intention to cause harm or steal users’ data.

The Play Store is the official app distribution store on Android. Apps are required to meet certain criteria to be hosted in the store. Additionally, Google performs security scans and checks to make sure that apps installed through the Play Store are safe. However, Google has its own set of rules that must be obeyed by developers who want their apps to be in the Play Store. If an app breaks any of those rules, it can be rejected from the store or have its approval revoked. Play Store rules are created to protect users, but there are restrictions that some apps cannot meet due to the features of the apps or how they work. There are app developers who decide willingly against submitting their apps to the Play Store, yet their apps can be completely safe, and the source code may be provided for anyone who wants to review it.

On the other hand, not having an app in the Play Store reduces the app’s reach, especially since it is always recommended to install apps from the Play Store as the safer choice for most users. People may also link the absence of a Play Store version to foul play, assuming that something prevents the app from gaining Google’s trust and being listed on the Play Store. As users should be more vigilant with accessibility services, it is understandable when a person refuses to install a screen reader that is not in the Play Store. However, not having a Play Store version does not directly translate to being a suspicious or risky app. There are apps that have functionalities that violate certain store restrictions, or simply apps whose developers don’t like to put their screen reader in the store. They could even opt for an open-source approach that is free from any store limitations, with both the updates and source code directly in the hands of users.

On the contrary, if a screen reader is on the Play Store, that doesn’t mean that it is completely risk-free, even if the risk is minimized. Bad actors are still able to sneak under Google’s verification mechanisms and land on the Play Store, with some apps gaining a high number of installs before being discovered. Additionally, accessibility services that are trusted by the Play Store could be doing shady things indirectly that affect users’ privacy.

It’s worth mentioning here that even if an app is sideloaded, when Play Protect is turned on, which it is by default, Play Protect scans the app for malicious software. If it identifies an app as potentially harmful, it can warn the user, disable or remove the app, or in some cases prevent it from being installed.

In order for a screen reader to be effective, it should work reliably without crashes and should be free of restrictions. Some Android UIs trust TalkBack as the built-in screen reader, giving it certain privileges that are not given to third-party screen readers, even if they are granted accessibility permission. Apps might also provide accessibility UI changes or expose data to TalkBack only, not to third-party screen readers.

For this reason, some screen readers spoof TalkBack by running their service and showing it to the system and other apps as the TalkBack package. Such behavior is not necessarily wrongdoing, even though an app generally shouldn’t try to make other apps believe that it is a different app, if the purpose is simply to enhance usability rather than to gain access to data for suspicious reasons.

Another example is when an app is given the ability to turn on and off other accessibility services. While this is not a straightforward process because it requires issuing ADB commands, it is still doable with the right knowledge. An app with such capability poses a serious risk, and I cannot imagine that it would be considered compliant with Google’s rules. But if the app is built to assist users in toggling between their screen readers, we look at the matter differently.

An example is the Shortcut Menu app, which is available on GitHub as an open-source project, and which I highly doubt could be approved for the Play Store if its developer decided to add it there. The app is built to give users an accessible way to switch between screen readers or to turn on another screen reader if one stops working as intended.

With the widespread use of AI, some screen readers allow the use of online AI services to describe content or perform OCR. They could also allow the use of non-AI services, such as translation or OCR. It is important to differentiate between the screen reader and the services it connects to. Third-party services are governed by the rules of the operators of those services, not by the screen reader utilizing them. This doesn’t mean that the screen reader is completely immune from responsibility. The screen reader should disclose the services it is connecting to, should encrypt data to ensure its safe transfer, should refrain from having any agreements with external services that allow user data to be misused, and should be transparent about everything it does regarding the data it sends.

Google TalkBack uses Gemini, which is also developed by Google, to describe and answer questions about content, but Google reassures users that the data is encrypted and deleted after the descriptions are received. Despite its bad reputation when it comes to user data, Google can be trusted with a matter like this one.

Unfortunately, this level of trust cannot be given to third-party screen readers. Jieshuo Screen Reader, for example, uses an online AI model from vivo to provide descriptions and answer user prompts, but there is no disclosure in the app itself of the exact model used or how the data is communicated. There is also no guarantee that the app would disclose if the AI service being used is changed.

As I am not a user of any other screen reader on the market, I cannot speak about how other screen readers deal with this subject. In all cases, using online services to analyse content should always be optional. If it is not, the user should at least be aware of the functionality that uses the external service so they can decide whether they want to use the screen reader or not.

Here, the advanced extension system found in the Jieshuo Screen Reader comes to mind. It allows users to run Lua scripts, which could be used to communicate with Android APIs, upload and download data from the internet, add, edit, and delete files and folders, and more. Just because the Jieshuo Screen Reader enables the use of Lua extensions doesn’t mean that it is responsible for the damage inflicted by malicious extensions. Users should be vigilant enough to avoid running extensions without trusting their creators, especially since these extensions and tools could be encrypted, so their code cannot be reviewed by the user, even if they have the knowledge to do so, or at least by one of the popular AI services that can review Lua code.

Jieshuo Screen Reader might be the only popular screen reader that allows for advanced extensions on Android, but Windows screen readers have this capability as well. If I am a user of NVDA and I decide to run an untrusted add-on, putting myself at risk, I am responsible for the risks I am knowingly exposing myself to.

With that being said, it is not possible to avoid criticizing how the extension threat is handled by the Jieshuo developer. All users can upload extensions to the Jieshuo servers, where they are discoverable by all Jieshuo users who go to the Extensions, Tools, or Gesture Scheme additional resources. Those codes are not vetted or checked, although their presence on the Jieshuo service could suggest otherwise to an unsuspecting beginner or average user. This user might go ahead and download an extension or tool, trusting its legitimacy, only to fall victim to a malicious one. Jieshuo Screen Reader poses a risk to those users, even if indirectly, because there should be a review of uploaded extensions and tools, or at least a clear warning when downloading those codes that they are not monitored.

They say that humans are the weakest link in cybersecurity, as many attacks are successful because of human error or reckless actions. With screen readers, the role of human error comes into play when installing unverified APKs. If you see a message on Telegram or WhatsApp that a new screen reader has been developed along with its APK, you don’t have to rush to install it. This could be malware waiting to take control of your device and data.

If you find someone posting about a new version of a screen reader you use, you don’t have to install and share this new version with others if you cannot trust the person who posted the APK. Popular screen readers have official places where they can be obtained. There are also reputable websites or channels that share official new versions when they are released.

Jieshuo Screen Reader, for example, is one of the screen readers that is widely shared in groups and channels, with modified versions sometimes being treated as official versions by users who think they are using the legitimate software when they are actually using a modified app. The screen reader has a GitHub page from which its releases can be downloaded, and new versions can also be downloaded through Jieshuo itself. There is also a website, although it is less known due to the lack of communication between the developer and the international user base.

Screen readers that are found on the Play Store are not immune either, as updates released through the Play Store can take more time to be approved and reach devices, and developers sometimes release versions as direct APKs before pushing them to the Play Store. When those APKs are modified and shared as the official versions, users may download them and put themselves at serious potential risk, something that could have been avoided simply by trying to find the official website or the screen reader developer’s channel.

Whenever an app hides some features behind a paywall, crackers try to use their skills to create and distribute pirated copies that allow users to access the Pro features without paying for them.

Putting aside the illegality and unethical nature of using cracked software, using a modified version of an app comes with the risk of malware being injected into it. This risk significantly increases when the app in question is an accessibility service like a screen reader.

The prominent example of a paid screen reader that is widely cracked is the Jieshuo Screen Reader , especially given the not-so-convenient method of purchase it utilizes . Maybe I won’t be exaggerating if I say that modified copies of Jieshuo are more widespread than official copies, with users sometimes even unable to differentiate between legitimate and modified copies. With so many cracked copies available, many users are put at risk of having their data stolen, as well as other damage that could result from running malware included in an accessibility service.

However, the screen reader’s developer cannot be held responsible for what a crack includes. In fact, the original developers are also victims, losing money due to unauthorized access to paid features, as well as suffering reputational damage because of the presence of cracked copies that could cause the original software to be flagged because of them.

A screen reader can monitor your banking activity. It can go further by silently entering data and simulating clicks without you even knowing what is happening, especially since a screen reader can alter the speech you hear or even perform operations without providing any speech feedback at all.

Many banking apps treat third-party accessibility services as potential threats, with some of them blocking them indiscriminately and others only allowing services that come from the Play Store. Others might flag a specific screen reader and refuse to run even if the screen reader is only installed but not running. While the measures banks take to protect users from unauthorized access and transfers are understandable, deciding whether what a bank does is an indication of wrongdoing by a screen reader is a different matter. First, the user must know why the screen reader is denied access and whether this is a measure applied to all third-party screen readers, to those that don’t come from the Play Store, or to a specific screen reader. If users are able to get the necessary information from their banks, something I doubt many banks would provide, their assessment of the security of the screen readers they use would be more objective and not based on assumptions or fear.

In all cases, denying access to banking apps and their data undermines the use of a screen reader, even if the user trusts that screen reader completely. I personally don’t like very strict measures such as blocking access to an app just because another app is present on the phone, since making sure that no unverified accessibility service is running while the user is in the bank’s app should be enough, as the user is free to use a certain screen reader elsewhere.

Some users might be very cautious when it comes to running third-party screen readers, especially those that are not in the Play Store, yet they might have a more relaxed attitude toward other types of apps that deal with sensitive data. TTS engines are one important example. Some people don’t realize that TTS engines can be used as a weapon against them and their security. A TTS engine that suddenly appears in a group or channel is still capable of logging every single character sent to it from other apps, including the screen reader. This data can be uploaded to external services, where it is analysed in search of potentially valuable information. With AI tools that can analyse huge sets of data quickly, going through generated speech output is now an easy task.

If you use TalkBack but have a TTS engine that is constantly consuming an unjustified amount of data, you should be concerned about your security, as the feeling of safety you have may be false.

Another category of apps that is popular these days is online image description and text recognition apps. Those apps connect to an external service, typically an AI one, where the data is sent and analysed to provide the information requested by the user. The number of these apps is increasing quickly, assisted by vibe coding, which makes app development easier than ever. The same points raised about screen readers communicating with external services are valid here, but there is also the fact that some users don’t think about what they are sending to those services through apps that are not considered risky accessibility services.

The previous examples are for apps specifically designed for blind people, but other apps can be security threats without requiring accessibility service access. They pose a risk to both sighted and blind people. For this reason, it is always recommended to check the permissions an app asks for, as well as any suspicious behaviour or unjustified use of a permission, such as access to the microphone or camera, or unusually high data consumption.

Opinions about the use of third-party screen readers differ within the blind community, with people at opposite ends of the spectrum.

On one hand, you find the highly cautious user who thinks that every third-party screen reader is a serious security risk, or even a spy agent harvesting every interaction, and should be avoided at any cost, with some applying this judgment only to screen readers that aren’t on the Play Store. While being reluctant to install potentially risky software is not a problem in itself, the issue starts when those people begin to make unsubstantiated claims. It is fine not to use a piece of software or not to like it, and to give your opinion about the risks of running an unverified accessibility service, but it is not fine to state your own thoughts as facts. Evaluating a software’s security can require procedures that include testing the software in a safe, sandboxed environment to analyse its behaviour and identify anything alarming.

On the other hand, you have the careless user who thinks that everything is safe. This is the user who doesn’t think for a minute before testing a screen reader, no matter where it comes from. This type of user is the one who argues that they don’t have anything to hide and that more cautious people are complicating the uncomplicated. Those users not only risk their own security and privacy, but they also risk the security and privacy of others, as we don’t live in a vacuum. We interact with other people through phones and tablets that could be running infected screen readers, and we connect to networks that could be subject to attacks. Those people increase the risk of data theft, impersonation to facilitate scamming others, and other forms of damage.

As with many other topics, our own subjective judgments play a role in whether we consider a screen reader secure and safe or not. Some people assume that a screen reader developed by someone from a certain country is a dangerous security threat, while one created by someone who resides in a country they trust is considered very safe. While it is true that some countries have better regulations and respect user rights more than others, criminal activities can be carried out anywhere. In fact, sometimes the reputation of a country’s strict laws can be a good cover for a bad actor to gain people’s trust. On the contrary, respect for users’ security and privacy can be found in the work of developers who might live in areas where the laws violate security and privacy. As they say, the person who knows the risk best is the person who has faced the risk.

Our biases are our own affairs that can affect what we trust and what we don’t trust, and it is a wise decision for someone who has escaped a totalitarian country not to use apps that come from developers in the country they ran away from. But we must present our statements as our subjective opinions, not as objective facts, if we are not willing or able to carry out the necessary evaluation procedures to determine what can be considered safe and what cannot.

I don’t have an answer to this question, nor is my goal to provide one. This article is an attempt to correct some misconceptions and raise awareness about accessibility services and what they can do. When you enable the accessibility service of a screen reader, you trust that screen reader, but at the same time, you agree that you are putting yourself under a theoretical risk. Those who follow my articles know that my primary screen reader of choice is Jieshuo , the notorious third-party screen reader. But many would not know that I remained reluctant to install this screen reader for years. Even now, I don’t have the confidence to tell people that this screen reader is completely innocent and safe, despite my personal opinion of it and my use of it.

I still have a tendency not to install new screen readers as soon as they are released, and I generally avoid screen readers that are neither on the Play Store nor open source. When it comes to open-source and closed-source screen readers, I lean toward an open-source screen reader free of Play Store limitations over a closed-source one found in the Play Store, provided I can identify its developers. Although I haven’t tested recent screen readers, I follow a few of them closely, with the possibility of installing them on my devices in the future. This doesn’t imply that I find the screen reader I use more secure than the screen readers I haven’t installed. In fact, the opposite could be true. Yet, I still stick to what I use because I have adapted my usage to the screen reader that I have used for years, without ignoring the possibility that something could go wrong one day.

Screen reader developers should be transparent about what data they collect, which external services they communicate with, and how they communicate with those services. When they offer advanced capabilities such as extensions,they should alert users to the risks of using unverified extensions instead of giving them a false sense of safety by letting them explore unvetted extensions or making it very easy to run extensions without any proper warning.

Whatever comes with the accessibility permission, restricting it is not the solution, as these restrictions cause more harm than they prevent. The solution lies in the hands of users, who should use common sense when they want to install a third-party accessibility service. Look at the gains versus the potential risks. Stay away from APKs from unknown sources, and don’t come near cracks. Keep Play Protect scanning for sideloaded apps enabled. Distinguish between the real risks of a screen reader and human error or recklessness. Look for any red flags, but don’t try to dictate your preferences as established facts.

news.title: WeWalk Smart Cane 2: la nueva generación del bastón inteligente ya está a la venta
news.summary: La tecnología aplicada a la movilidad de las personas ciegas y con baja visión continúa avanzando. Una de las novedades que ha llegado es el WeWalk Smart Cane 2, la nueva generación del bastón inteligente desarrollado por WeWalk, que incorpora mejoras en detección de obstáculos, navegación, controles físicos y asistencia mediante inteligencia artificial. El nuevo […] La entrada WeWalk Smart Cane 2: la nueva generación del bastón inteligente ya está a la venta se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
La tecnología aplicada a la movilidad de las personas ciegas y con baja visión continúa avanzando. Una de las novedades que ha llegado es el WeWalk Smart Cane 2 , la nueva generación del bastón inteligente desarrollado por WeWalk, que incorpora mejoras en detección de obstáculos, navegación, controles físicos y asistencia mediante inteligencia artificial.

El nuevo dispositivo ya está en el mercado y ya está siendo presentado en diferentes eventos europeos de tecnología asistiva. En octubre podrá probarse, por ejemplo, en eventos especializados celebrados en Dublín y Londres.

El WeWalk Smart Cane 2 mantiene la utilización del bastón blanco como herramienta principal de movilidad, pero añade sensores y funciones digitales para proporcionar información adicional al usuario.

Una de sus funciones principales es la detección de obstáculos situados por encima del nivel del suelo , como ramas, señales u otros elementos que podrían encontrarse a la altura del pecho o de la cabeza.

La compañía afirma que el nuevo modelo mejora un 30 % la precisión y el enfoque de la detección de obstáculos respecto a la generación anterior.

Es importante señalar que esta función no sustituye las técnicas tradicionales de utilización del bastón. El propio fabricante indica que el sensor no está diseñado para detectar desniveles, escalones, bordillos o agujeros en el suelo, por lo que continúa siendo necesario utilizar correctamente el bastón blanco para detectar este tipo de elementos.

Una de las modificaciones más visibles está en el propio diseño del dispositivo.

El Smart Cane 2 es aproximadamente un 25 % más ligero y un 40 % más delgado que su predecesor. Además, incorpora resistencia frente a las condiciones meteorológicas y una nueva disposición de los controles.

Mientras que el primer WeWalk utilizaba una superficie táctil, el nuevo modelo apuesta por botones físicos , algo que puede facilitar la interacción y hacer que determinadas funciones sean más fáciles de localizar mediante el tacto.

El fabricante también ha incorporado un altavoz tres veces más potente que el del modelo anterior y una linterna integrada.

Las alertas pueden recibirse mediante sonido y vibración , con diferentes posibilidades de personalización.

Una de las funciones más interesantes del ecosistema WeWalk es la navegación mediante voz.

Cuando el bastón está conectado al teléfono móvil y a la aplicación WeWalk, el usuario puede recibir indicaciones paso a paso para desplazarse hasta diferentes destinos.

El sistema también proporciona información relacionada con el transporte público. Entre otras posibilidades, puede informar sobre rutas y ayudar a seguir un trayecto en transporte público, incluyendo avisos relacionados con el momento en el que hay que bajarse.

Esta función puede resultar especialmente interesante en desplazamientos por entornos desconocidos, ya que permite recibir las indicaciones directamente desde el bastón sin tener que sostener el teléfono.

El modelo básico tiene un precio de 699 € e incluye las principales funciones inteligentes del bastón, como la detección de obstáculos elevados, la conectividad con el teléfono móvil y las funciones de navegación.

También existe la posibilidad de añadir una suscripción anual de 129 € que incorpora las funciones de inteligencia artificial y sus correspondientes mejoras.

Además, WeWALK ofrece la posibilidad de reservar una clase online de formación para aprender a utilizar el dispositivo , con un precio de 129 €.

En cuanto a la adaptación física, el bastón puede personalizarse según la altura de la persona usuaria, con medidas disponibles desde 119 hasta 150 centímetros , para conseguir un ajuste más adecuado a cada usuario.

Otra de las grandes novedades del Smart Cane 2 es la incorporación de un asistente de inteligencia artificial basado en Gemini .

La interacción se realiza mediante voz y permite formular preguntas relacionadas con el entorno o solicitar información.

Según WeWalk, el asistente puede utilizarse, por ejemplo, para:

De esta manera, el bastón incorpora una capa adicional de asistencia basada en inteligencia artificial, que se suma a las funciones de movilidad y navegación.

El nuevo dispositivo se comercializa en dos configuraciones.

Por un lado está el WeWalk Smart Cane 2 , que incorpora las funciones principales de detección de obstáculos, navegación, información sobre transporte público, lugares cercanos, iluminación y conectividad con el teléfono.

Por otro lado, el WeWalk Smart Cane 2 AI añade acceso ilimitado al asistente de inteligencia artificial integrado.

También es posible adquirir el modelo estándar y añadir posteriormente el acceso al asistente mediante una suscripción.

Aunque el Smart Cane 2 incorpora sensores y funciones avanzadas, WeWalk insiste en que debe utilizarse manteniendo las técnicas habituales de movilidad con bastón.

El sistema de detección de obstáculos está pensado para proporcionar información adicional, pero no puede detectar todos los peligros presentes en el entorno. Por ejemplo, la propia documentación del dispositivo advierte de que el sensor no detecta desniveles del terreno como escaleras, bordillos o agujeros.

Por este motivo, el Smart Cane 2 debe entenderse como una herramienta complementaria al bastón blanco tradicional , no como un dispositivo que sustituya la formación en orientación y movilidad.

El WeWalk Smart Cane 2 refleja una tendencia cada vez más presente en la tiflotecnología: la incorporación de sensores, navegación, conectividad móvil e inteligencia artificial en dispositivos que las personas ciegas ya utilizan habitualmente.

Su llegada prevista para noviembre permitirá comprobar cómo responden las personas usuarias a esta combinación de movilidad tradicional, detección de obstáculos, navegación mediante voz e inteligencia artificial .

El nuevo modelo ya está siendo mostrado en eventos especializados de tecnología asistiva y se espera su lanzamiento comercial a principios de noviembre de 2026.

news.title: Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3
news.summary: Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación, la beta 4 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, … Continuar leyendo "Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3" La entrada Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .
news.body:
Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación , la beta 4 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, o por el sistema de informe de fallos de NV Access . Esta versión no es apta para entornos de producción. Al instalar esta beta te unirás al canal beta, y sólo recibirás avisos de actualización de compilaciones beta y candidatas a liberación (rc). El canal beta/rc siempre te mantendrá al día con la versión más reciente de NVDA. La última rc de un ciclo de liberación es idéntica a la última versión estable. Para regresar al canal de versiones estables, instala a mano la última versión estable.

Esta versión incorpora importantes mejoras de rendimiento, mejoras en los diálogos de NVDA, y entrada expandida por la pantalla táctil. Se han hecho varias mejoras para reducir los retrasos y aumentar el rendimiento. Ahora NVDA recupera y captura más información sobre los controles en segundo plano, mejorando el rendimiento en controles como cuadros combinados y el explorador de archivos. NVDA ya no hace que se rompan el explorador de archivos u otras aplicaciones al cerrarlo o reiniciarlo. NVDA se recupera ahora más rápido cuando una aplicación deja de responder, y ya no se colgará ni inundará el registro con errores en aplicaciones que no responden. En regiones vivas de texto, como las terminales, NVDA ya no se cuelga cuando se vuelcan en pantalla importantes cantidades de texto. Se han añadido menús de contexto y atajos de teclado a los diálogos de perfiles de configuración, gestos de entrada y diccionarios del habla, haciendo que estos diálogos sean más fáciles de usar con el teclado. Ahora también es posible cambiar directamente un gesto existente en el diálogo Gestos de entrada. Se ha modernizado el diálogo que presenta mensajes explorables y ahora soporta mejor cambiar su tamaño, maximizarlo y minimizarlo. Se ha expandido significativamente la entrada por pantalla táctil. Los gestos de dos deslizamientos secuenciales ahora combinan dos deslizamientos en rápida sucesión en un solo gesto, incrementando enormemente la cantidad de gestos asociables. También se soportan ahora los gestos de borde, permitiendo que los gestos que comiencen a 15 mm de cualquier borde de la pantalla se asocien independientemente de los mismos gestos realizados en el centro de la pantalla. Se ha añadido una nueva orden sin asignar para mover el cursor del ratón al centro de la vista ampliada. Se puede usar el OCR de Windows con la lupa o la cortina de pantalla activadas. Se ha actualizado Liblouis con nuevas tablas braille en Elfdaliano, sami, maorí, braille unificado inglés de Nueva Zelanda, y aitiano criollo, una tabla noruega para texto en español, y variantes adicionales de sueco de 6 y 8 puntos. Se ha actualizado Espeak NG añadiendo soporte para liguriano y abkhaz. Para instalar esta beta, puedes configurar el canal «rc y beta» en el complemento Selector del canal de actualización y buscar actualizaciones desde el menú Ayuda de NVDA, o actualizar desde una beta anterior. Y como siempre, también puedes descargar manualmente el instalador de NVDA 2026.3 beta 4 . Su suma de comprobación SHA256, que te permitirá garantizar la integridad del archivo descargado, es 8be91476179710c4abffe5094459df9be1696d92e5d6cd0ace47d52321bb87ab. ¡Feliz martes!

La entrada Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .

news.title: Monarch 2.0 lleva la IA al braille y los gráficos táctiles
news.summary: HumanWare ha lanzado Monarch 2.0, una importante actualización de su dispositivo de braille multilineal y gráficos táctiles, con nuevas funciones de inteligencia artificial y mejoras para explorar matemáticas, gráficos y contenidos digitales. El Monarch combina 10 líneas de braille con gráficos táctiles dinámicos en una misma superficie, permitiendo acceder mediante el tacto a información que […] La entrada Monarch 2.0 lleva la IA al braille y los gráficos táctiles se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
HumanWare ha lanzado Monarch 2.0, una importante actualización de su dispositivo de braille multilineal y gráficos táctiles, con nuevas funciones de inteligencia artificial y mejoras para explorar matemáticas, gráficos y contenidos digitales.

El Monarch combina 10 líneas de braille con gráficos táctiles dinámicos en una misma superficie , permitiendo acceder mediante el tacto a información que tradicionalmente se presenta de forma visual. La actualización 2.0 fue anunciada por HumanWare el 14 de septiembre de 2026.

Monarch es un dispositivo de tecnología de apoyo desarrollado por HumanWare en colaboración con la American Printing House for the Blind (APH) y la National Federation of the Blind (NFB) .

Su característica principal es combinar braille multilineal y gráficos táctiles en una única pantalla dinámica. El dispositivo cuenta con 10 líneas de 32 celdas de braille , además de una superficie formada por miles de puntos que permite representar información gráfica mediante el tacto.

De esta forma, una persona puede explorar mediante el tacto textos, diagramas, mapas, gráficos y contenidos matemáticos , sin depender exclusivamente de materiales impresos o gráficos táctiles estáticos.

Una de las novedades de Monarch 2.0 es Describe with AI , una función capaz de generar una descripción verbal de una imagen .

Esta herramienta se incorpora al visor de gráficos táctiles y permite obtener información mediante una descripción generada por inteligencia artificial.

La función puede resultar especialmente interesante cuando se trabaja con contenidos que contienen información visual y puede complementar la exploración táctil.

No obstante, HumanWare no presenta Describe with AI como un sustituto de la representación táctil . Se trata de una función de descripción de imágenes integrada en el dispositivo.

Monarch 2.0 también incorpora mejoras destinadas a facilitar el acceso a información matemática y gráfica.

El visor de gráficos KeyMath ha sido rediseñado para ofrecer más detalle y simplificar la exploración de gráficos. Además, la integración de MathCAT mejora la conversión de contenidos matemáticos entre la representación impresa y el braille.

Por otro lado, Tactile Viewer incorpora nuevos niveles de zoom para determinados gráficos, incluidos los archivos SVG .

Esto permite ampliar las posibilidades de exploración de diagramas y otros contenidos gráficos mediante el tacto.

Las nuevas funciones pueden tener especial interés en el ámbito educativo.

El Monarch está diseñado para que estudiantes ciegos y con baja visión puedan acceder a contenidos que tradicionalmente presentan importantes barreras de accesibilidad, como gráficos, mapas, diagramas, ecuaciones o libros de texto digitales .

La actualización también incorpora un modo examen , que permite al personal educativo seleccionar qué aplicaciones y herramientas puede utilizar el estudiante durante una evaluación.

De esta manera, el alumno puede seguir utilizando las capacidades de braille y gráficos táctiles del Monarch mientras se restringe el acceso a determinadas herramientas durante una prueba.

Monarch 2.0 introduce mejoras en el intercambio y la colaboración mediante KeyDrive y añade estilos integrados para archivos eBraille en VictorReader.

Estas mejoras buscan facilitar el acceso a documentos digitales y ampliar las posibilidades de trabajo con contenidos en braille electrónico.

La evolución del Monarch muestra cómo diferentes tecnologías de apoyo pueden combinarse en un mismo dispositivo.

Hasta ahora, acceder a determinados contenidos visuales podía requerir disponer de un gráfico táctil específicamente preparado. Con Monarch, los usuarios pueden explorar gráficos dinámicos y braille en una misma superficie, mientras que Describe with AI añade una vía adicional para obtener información verbal sobre imágenes .

Para ámbitos como la educación, las matemáticas, la lectura de gráficos o el acceso a información visual, esta combinación puede abrir nuevas posibilidades de interacción con contenidos digitales.

La actualización Monarch 2.0 ya ha sido anunciada por HumanWare y amplía las funciones del dispositivo con herramientas centradas en braille, gráficos táctiles, matemáticas e inteligencia artificial.

news.title: Shortcut Menu
news.summary: Shortcut Menu lets the Android accessibility shortcut, such as holding both volume keys, turn your choice of screen reader or other accessibility service on or…
news.body:
Published 3 October 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Shortcut Menu lets the Android accessibility shortcut, such as holding both volume keys, turn your choice of screen reader or other accessibility service on or off. It works like the accessibility shortcut menu on iPhone:

Turning a screen reader on turns any other screen reader off, so two never talk at once. Services with the same name, such as Google’s and Samsung’s TalkBack, are told apart by their maker, such as “TalkBack (Samsung)”. Pressing the shortcut again while the menu is open closes it.

Without Shortcut Menu, a shortcut with more than one feature on it asks which one to use, and that question is not spoken when no screen reader is on.

With Shizuku, run the same command without adb shell. In Settings, Accessibility, open Shortcut Menu and turn on its shortcut, such as the volume keys. Make Shortcut Menu the only feature on that shortcut. Open the Shortcut Menu app and choose which services the menu offers. Until you choose, it offers your screen readers. The app also shows whether the permission is granted and what each shortcut is assigned to, and has a button to try the menu. How it works The shortcut turns Shortcut Menu’s accessibility service on, and the service opens the menu. When the menu closes, the service turns itself off, so the next press turns it on again. A press while the menu is open turns the service off, which closes the menu.

Choosing a service changes Android’s list of enabled accessibility services directly, so Android does not ask “Allow full control?” each time. The menu speaks with the phone’s text-to-speech engine, at the accessibility volume.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Samsung UI is the only Android UI that offers 3 accessibility shortcuts: pressing and holding the volume keys, short pressing the power and volume up keys, and the accessibility onscreen button or gesture, based on the navigation mode being used. Other OEMs offer only the first and third shortcuts. Honor even excludes the accessibility button and gesture, leaving the user with only 1 shortcut, and that shortcut can only be assigned to 1 accessibility service. On UIs that allow more than 1 accessibility service to be assigned to the shortcut, Android asks the user to choose which one to activate every time the shortcut is used. However, this dialog is not accessible if no screen reader is running.

Shortcut Menu aims to address these shortcomings by allowing the user to choose the accessibility services they want to launch from the shortcut. The user can then launch any of the selected services in an accessible way. When no screen reader is active, the service speaks the items as the user moves their finger over them, and lifting the finger activates the selected service. If a screen reader is already active, the service makes sure to turn it off before launching another screen reader to avoid potential conflicts.

Setting up the app requires an ADB command, which can be run either using ADB on a computer or directly on the phone through an ADB app that uses wireless debugging. Working with ADB is not covered here, but I personally used the ADB AppControl mobile app to enter the command that grants the app the required permission.

The app's UI is straightforward. It shows whether the permission has been granted and which shortcut is assigned to the service. It also includes a menu where you can turn services on or off without using the shortcut. The user can select which services should be included, although screen readers are checked by default. For me, Jieshuo Main, Jieshuo Helper Service, TalkBack, and AI Subtitles were all included.

When using the shortcut, the app currently speaks through Google TTS. When a screen reader is active, it behaves like a regular screen that the screen reader can interact with.

For Samsung users who keep both Samsung TalkBack and Google's TalkBack on their devices and wish to switch between them, both can be added to the services list. I haven't tested this on a Samsung device to see if there are any issues. Anyway, starting with One UI 9, Samsung TalkBack is replaced with Google TalkBack, so there are no longer two TalkBack versions.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

App version: 0.2, Android 16

news.title: DelveKin: Dungeon Defense
news.summary: The heroes are coming. Build a dungeon worthy of stopping them! DelveKin is a charming dungeon defense strategy game where you take the role of the Dungeon Master. Design your defenses, place traps, command monsters, and battle invading heroes across handcrafted encounters and replay-able dungeon challenges. BUILD YOUR DUNGEON - Choose rooms with different layouts and tactical advantages, then fill them with monsters and traps. Every placement matters as heroes advance deeper into your dungeon. COMMAND YOUR MONSTERS - Take direct control during turn-based battles. Move across the battlefield, launch basic attacks, unleash special abilities, and combine your monsters' strengths to overcome each group of heroes. SET CLEVER TRAPS - Slow heroes with snares, strike from the walls with arrow slits, or punish careless movement with hidden hazards. Traps can shape the battlefield and create opportunities for your monsters. GROW YOUR ARSENAL - Unlock new monsters, traps, rooms, and powerful bosses as you progress. Earn experience, level up your defenses, and build stronger dungeon teams for the challenges ahead. FACE NEW HEROES - Each stage introduces different hero combinations, abilities, and tactical threats. Adapt your dungeon to withstand knights, mages, rogues, clerics, and other determined adventurers. VENTURE INTO DEEP DELVE - Put your dungeon building skills to the ultimate test in Deep Delve, a replay-able 20-depth challenge where every run is different. Build a run specific roster, recruit and replace monsters and traps, choose powerful upgrades, evolve your boss, and see how deep your dungeon can survive. CONTINUE INTO DUNGEON RAIDS - Complete the main campaign and enter Dungeon Raids, where increasingly dangerous hero parties push your defenses even further. CHARMING ART STYLE - DelveKin features expressive characters, lively battle animations, and a playful fantasy world. Play the opening chapters for free. A single Premium unlock opens the full campaign, additional progression, Dungeon Raids, and Deep Delve. Build carefully. Fight cleverly. Protect your dungeon.

news.title: LUCID: inteligencia artificial para aprender Braille
news.summary: La inteligencia artificial también está abriendo nuevas posibilidades en el aprendizaje del Braille. Un ejemplo es LUCID, un sistema de aprendizaje diseñado por el Product Experience Design Lab (PXD Lab) de la Universidad de Houston, en Estados Unidos. La propuesta combina interacción táctil, una pantalla Braille y orientación mediante audio asistida por inteligencia artificial. Su […] La entrada LUCID: inteligencia artificial para aprender Braille se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
La inteligencia artificial también está abriendo nuevas posibilidades en el aprendizaje del Braille. Un ejemplo es LUCID , un sistema de aprendizaje diseñado por el Product Experience Design Lab (PXD Lab) de la Universidad de Houston , en Estados Unidos.

La propuesta combina interacción táctil, una pantalla Braille y orientación mediante audio asistida por inteligencia artificial . Su objetivo es acompañar a las personas ciegas y con baja visión desde el aprendizaje de las primeras letras hasta la práctica de la lectura.

El proyecto ha recibido además un Red Dot Award en la categoría de Inclusive Design , un reconocimiento internacional relacionado con el diseño de soluciones innovadoras.

LUCID es un concepto de tecnología asistiva para el aprendizaje del Braille desarrollado por el equipo del PXD Lab de la Universidad de Houston.

El sistema está formado por dos dispositivos complementarios: LUCID-ALT y LUCID-ARC . Cada uno está pensado para una etapa diferente del aprendizaje.

La idea es que la persona pueda avanzar progresivamente, comenzando por el reconocimiento de los caracteres Braille y pasando después a ejercicios de lectura con una pantalla Braille de tamaño real.

La primera parte del sistema es LUCID-ALT .

Se trata de un dispositivo con un teclado ampliado de seis puntos , basado en la estructura de la celda Braille. El usuario puede explorar mediante el tacto las diferentes combinaciones de puntos y familiarizarse con la formación de las letras.

Este planteamiento pone el tacto en el centro del aprendizaje , en lugar de sustituir la experiencia Braille por una interacción exclusivamente sonora.

A medida que la persona progresa, el sistema plantea una transición hacia una experiencia de lectura más cercana a la que encontrará posteriormente en una pantalla Braille convencional.

La segunda parte es LUCID-ARC , que incorpora una pantalla Braille de tamaño real .

Su función es permitir que el aprendizaje avance desde el reconocimiento de letras hacia la práctica de la lectura. De esta manera, el usuario no se queda únicamente en ejercicios básicos con los seis puntos, sino que puede familiarizarse progresivamente con una experiencia de lectura más próxima a la de otros dispositivos Braille.

Según la Universidad de Houston, esta transición pretende preparar al estudiante para las herramientas que utilizará fuera del proceso de aprendizaje.

Uno de los elementos más llamativos de LUCID es la incorporación de inteligencia artificial como apoyo durante el aprendizaje .

El sistema utiliza orientaciones y comentarios de audio en tiempo real para acompañar al usuario mientras realiza los ejercicios. La intención es ofrecer indicaciones durante la práctica y reducir la necesidad de contar continuamente con un instructor al lado.

De esta forma, LUCID combina dos vías de interacción:

La Universidad de Houston explica que esta combinación busca favorecer una práctica más autónoma y permitir que cada estudiante avance a su propio ritmo.

Uno de los aspectos más interesantes de LUCID es que no plantea la inteligencia artificial como sustituta del Braille.

Al contrario, el sistema mantiene la experiencia táctil como elemento fundamental y utiliza la IA como apoyo durante el proceso de aprendizaje.

Esto resulta especialmente relevante en un contexto en el que cada vez existen más herramientas tecnológicas basadas en voz. Para las personas ciegas y con baja visión, la tecnología puede facilitar el acceso a la información, pero el Braille continúa siendo una herramienta fundamental para la alfabetización, la lectura y la escritura.

La propuesta de LUCID busca precisamente combinar ambos mundos: la información sonora que puede proporcionar la inteligencia artificial y la información táctil que proporciona el Braille .

El proyecto ha sido reconocido con un Red Dot Award en la categoría de Inclusive Design .

El reconocimiento corresponde al trabajo de la diseñadora Varshini Chouthri y del profesor Min Kang , director del Product Experience Design Lab de la Universidad de Houston.

Para el PXD Lab, este reconocimiento se suma a otros proyectos relacionados con el diseño centrado en las personas y la tecnología.

Es importante hacer una aclaración.

LUCID no debe confundirse con un producto comercial que ya pueda adquirirse. La información publicada por la Universidad de Houston presenta el proyecto como un sistema diseñado por su laboratorio y muestra representaciones del dispositivo. No hemos encontrado información oficial que indique que esté actualmente disponible para su compra o implantado de forma generalizada en centros educativos.

Por tanto, hablamos de una propuesta de diseño y tecnología asistiva , no de un producto que actualmente podamos recomendar para aprender Braille.

LUCID forma parte de una tendencia más amplia: el desarrollo de herramientas de inteligencia artificial que pueden utilizarse como apoyo para las personas ciegas y con baja visión.

La American Foundation for the Blind (AFB) ha analizado durante 2026 el uso de inteligencia artificial por parte de personas con discapacidad. Sus investigaciones muestran que la IA ya se utiliza para tareas como leer textos, describir imágenes y facilitar el acceso a información, aunque también advierten de problemas relacionados con la accesibilidad, la precisión y la necesidad de supervisión humana.

En este contexto, propuestas como LUCID muestran otra posibilidad: utilizar la IA no solamente para describir el mundo visual , sino también para acompañar procesos de aprendizaje relacionados con la tecnología asistiva .

La evolución de la tiflotecnología no consiste únicamente en desarrollar gafas inteligentes, aplicaciones de navegación o herramientas capaces de reconocer imágenes.

También implica buscar nuevas formas de aprender, leer y escribir de manera accesible .

LUCID plantea precisamente esta combinación entre Braille, tecnología háptica, audio e inteligencia artificial . Aunque todavía no se trata de una solución comercial disponible para el público, su diseño muestra una posible dirección para las futuras herramientas de aprendizaje accesible.

La tecnología puede cambiar la forma en la que utilizamos el Braille, pero propuestas como LUCID ponen el foco en algo fundamental: la tecnología debe servir para facilitar el acceso al aprendizaje sin dejar de lado la experiencia táctil que hace posible la lectura y escritura Braille.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuentes: University Of Houston , Red Dot , UhnPlus .
